The correct answer is D (Reporting lag means recent claims are not all reported yet, understating the true count.): Claims are often reported to an insurer with some delay after the loss occurs, so the most recent period in any extract is typically incomplete because not all eligible claims have yet been reported. Calendar length differences between months are far too small to explain the kind of artificial drop typically observed near the end of a claims extract. This reporting lag issue is a well known data design consideration that often requires either truncating the most recent period or applying a development adjustment.
  57. The correct answer is C (Avoiding chartjunk, since decorative elements that do not convey data only distract from the message.): Chartjunk refers to unnecessary decorative elements, such as 3D effects, background images, or excessive gridlines, that add visual clutter without conveying any additional information about the data. Removing these elements typically makes the actual data pattern easier for a reader to perceive quickly and accurately. Bar charts remain entirely appropriate for categorical variables like state, so the underlying chart type choice is not the issue here.
  58. The correct answer is B (The proportional ink principle, since ink used should be directly proportional to the data values.): The proportional ink principle states that the visual area or ink used to represent a value should scale proportionally with the value itself. Varying both width and height to represent a single quantity causes the visual area to scale with the square of the underlying value, exaggerating differences between bars. Bar charts remain a perfectly appropriate choice for representing counts; the problem lies specifically in how the bars are drawn, not in the chart type selected.
  59. The correct answer is C (Side by side boxplots, since they summarize the median, spread, and outliers for each group compactly.): Boxplots are specifically designed to summarize a continuous variable's central tendency, spread, and outliers, and placing them side by side allows direct comparison across the four vehicle type groups. A pie chart cannot convey spread or outliers at all, since it only shows proportions of a whole. Connecting categories with a line chart implies a false continuous ordering, and plotting a variable against itself provides no meaningful comparative information.
  60. The correct answer is C (A misleading axis, since a truncated baseline exaggerates the visual difference between the compared values.): Truncating the vertical axis away from zero is a classic technique that visually exaggerates small differences between bars, since the bar heights no longer scale proportionally with the underlying values. This particular problem is about axis construction, not about decorative clutter, chart type choice, or differing time frames of the compared data. Best practice for bar charts is generally to start the axis at zero unless there is a clearly stated and well justified reason not to.
  61. The correct answer is D (Human perception struggles to accurately compare small differences in angle across many similarly sized slices.): Research on visual perception shows that people are generally less accurate at comparing angles or areas than at comparing lengths or positions along a common scale, which becomes especially problematic when many slices are similarly sized. Pie charts can technically display more than two categories, though doing so with many similarly sized slices undermines their readability. A well constructed bar chart ordered by value is often a clearer alternative for this kind of comparison across several categories.
  62. The correct answer is B (A line chart, since it clearly conveys trend and ordering across a sequence of time periods.): Line charts naturally convey ordering and trend over time by connecting sequential points, making them well suited to displaying how a metric evolves across many consecutive periods. A pie chart discards the temporal ordering entirely and only shows relative shares at a single point, which is not the goal here. A single combined boxplot would lose the period by period detail that the actuary specifically wants to display.
  63. The correct answer is C (The proportional ink principle, since area rather than height should represent frequency when bin widths differ.): When histogram bins have unequal widths, the bar area rather than the bar height should represent the count or density in that bin, or else wider bins will visually appear to contain disproportionately more data. This is a direct application of the proportional ink principle to histogram construction specifically. Claim amount remains a ratio scaled continuous variable regardless of this display issue, and the problem has nothing to do with how the underlying data was sampled.
  64. The correct answer is C (It highlights the overall pattern, making it easier to see beyond the scatter of individual points.): A trend line summarizes the general direction and shape of the relationship, helping a viewer perceive the overall pattern that might otherwise be obscured by noise in individual data points. Adding a trend line has no effect on the underlying variable types of age or premium, which remain continuous. It also does not eliminate the value of examining individual points for outliers, nor does any statistical relationship shown in a scatterplot establish causation on its own.
  65. The correct answer is A (Whether the goal is to compare totals across regions or individual year values within each region.): Stacked bar charts are useful when the primary interest is comparing total claim counts across regions, since the segments sum to a meaningful overall total. Grouped bar charts, by contrast, make it easier to directly compare individual year values within each region since the bars sit side by side rather than stacked. The variable's scale type, the sampling method used to collect the underlying data, and the raw collection frequency are all much less relevant to this particular visualization choice.
  66. The correct answer is A (A sequential color scheme conveys the natural ordering of categories, unlike a rainbow gradient.): A sequential color palette, moving from light to dark within a single hue, naturally mirrors the increasing order of an ordinal variable's categories, helping viewers intuitively grasp the ranking. A rainbow gradient cycles through many distinct hues with no inherent perceptual ordering, which can actually obscure the ordinal structure of the data. Sequential palettes are specifically recommended for ordered variables, while qualitative palettes with distinct hues are more suited to nominal variables without inherent order.
  67. The correct answer is C (Every visual element should serve the data, and elements that add no information should be removed.): Good graph design generally follows the principle that every visual element on a chart should serve some informational purpose, and elements that only add decoration without conveying data should be minimized or removed. Multiple font styles, drop shadows, and background patterns are classic examples of chartjunk that distract from rather than support the data being communicated. This principle applies regardless of the scale type of the underlying variable or how many variables are being displayed at once.
  68. The correct answer is A (A log scale compresses extreme values so patterns among smaller, typical severities remain visible.): When a variable is heavily right skewed, a small number of very large values on a linear axis can compress all the smaller, more common values into a tiny region that is hard to interpret. Applying a log scale spreads out the smaller values while compressing the larger ones, often making patterns across the full range of typical claim severities much easier to see. A log scale is purely a visualization or transformation tool and does not change the underlying scale type classification of the variable itself, nor does it require any particular sampling method.
  69. The correct answer is A (It allows patterns and concentrations across two categorical dimensions to be spotted visually and quickly.): A heat map encodes numeric values as color intensity, which allows a viewer to spot patterns, concentrations, or unusual cells across two categorical dimensions much more quickly than scanning a table of raw numbers. The underlying counts still need to be computed to produce the heat map in the first place, so this benefit is purely about presentation rather than eliminating computation. A heat map is simply a visualization of the cross tabulation and has no bearing on whether the two categorical variables are actually statistically independent.
  70. The correct answer is C (Different variable types, such as categorical versus continuous, are best conveyed by different visual encodings.): Categorical variables are typically best displayed with bar charts or cross tabulations that group observations into discrete categories, while continuous variables are better suited to histograms, boxplots, or scatterplots that convey a range of values and shape. Choosing a chart type without regard to the underlying variable type risks either misrepresenting the data or obscuring important patterns such as distribution shape. This connection between variable type and appropriate visualization is a core principle taught for effective exploratory data analysis, not merely aesthetic preference.
  71. The correct answer is D (Viewers may misjudge the relative magnitude of the two regions since the axes are not comparable.): When two charts intended for direct visual comparison use different axis scales, a viewer glancing at bar heights alone may draw an inaccurate conclusion about relative magnitude between the two regions. This risk exists specifically because side by side comparison implicitly invites the viewer to compare visual size across the two charts as though the scales matched. The scale type classification of the underlying frequency variable and the technical definition of a bar chart are unaffected by this axis inconsistency.
  72. The correct answer is B (Right skewed, since the tail extends toward higher values while the bulk sits at lower values.): A distribution is described as right skewed, or positively skewed, when its longer tail extends toward higher values while the majority of observations cluster at lower values, exactly as described here. This shape is extremely common for claim severity data in practice, since most claims are modest while a small number are unusually large. A single tail extending in one direction is the definition of skewness, not of bimodality, which instead refers to the presence of two separate peaks in the distribution.
  73. The correct answer is A (Potential outliers, values that fall beyond a typical range defined relative to the interquartile range.): Boxplots typically define whiskers extending to the most extreme values within some multiple, commonly 1.5 times, of the interquartile range, and points beyond that range are plotted individually as potential outliers. The median is represented by a line inside the box itself, not by individually plotted points beyond the whiskers. Being flagged as a potential outlier does not automatically mean a value is an error; further investigation is generally needed before deciding whether to exclude or adjust such points.
  74. The correct answer is B (The distribution is right skewed, since a few unusually large values pull the mean upward.): The mean is sensitive to extreme values, so when a small number of very large claims exist, they pull the mean upward while the median, which depends only on the middle ranked observations, remains relatively unaffected. This pattern of mean exceeding median is a classic signature of right skewness rather than left skewness. There is no requirement that mean and median be equal in general, and a gap between them does not by itself imply the existence of two separate peaks.
  75. The correct answer is D (The median, since it depends only on the middle ranked values, not on extreme values.): The median is determined solely by the position of the middle observation or observations once the data is sorted, so it is largely unaffected by how extreme the highest or lowest values happen to be. The mean, by contrast, incorporates the actual magnitude of every observation, so unusually large values can pull it substantially away from where most of the data actually lies. Both the range and the standard deviation are directly influenced by extreme values, making them less robust than the median in this context.
  76. The correct answer is D (Bimodal, since the distribution displays two separate peaks rather than a single central tendency.): A bimodal distribution is one that displays two distinct peaks or modes, often suggesting the presence of two underlying subgroups within the overall population, such as new and long tenured policyholders here. Histograms can display any number of peaks depending on the underlying data, so unimodality is not guaranteed by definition. Skewness and bimodality are separate concepts, and a uniform distribution is actually characterized by having no pronounced peak at all, with roughly equal density across its range.
  77. The correct answer is C (Constructing a boxplot or histogram to see where extreme values fall relative to typical data.): Visualizing the data with a boxplot or histogram allows an analyst to see exactly how far extreme values sit from the bulk of typical observations and whether there is a plausible gap suggesting a distinct group or a data entry issue. Computing a mean from only the two extreme values would not provide any information about the distribution as a whole. Reclassifying a naturally continuous variable as nominal would discard meaningful quantitative information rather than address the underlying question of whether extreme values are valid.
  78. The correct answer is B (The range between the first and third quartiles, capturing the middle fifty percent of the data.): The interquartile range is defined as the distance between the first quartile and the third quartile, meaning it captures the central fifty percent of the sorted data. This differs entirely from the full range, which spans from the absolute minimum to the absolute maximum and is far more sensitive to extreme values. The interquartile range also does not represent any gap between mean and median, nor is it the same measure as standard deviation, even though both describe spread in some sense.
  79. The correct answer is D (Overdispersion relative to a simple Poisson assumption, which may motivate considering a negative binomial model instead.): For count data modeled with a Poisson distribution, the mean and variance are theoretically equal, so a variance substantially larger than the mean is a common sign of overdispersion. This observation frequently motivates actuaries to consider alternative distributions, such as the negative binomial, that can accommodate variance exceeding the mean. This pattern is a well documented feature of many real insurance datasets and does not by itself indicate a coding error, a change in variable type, or biased sampling.
  80. The correct answer is D (Investigate the isolated observations further to determine whether they reflect valid extreme values or data errors.): An isolated cluster of observations separated from the main body of the distribution warrants closer investigation before any action is taken, since it could represent legitimate but rare high premium policies or, alternatively, a data quality issue. Deleting such observations without investigation risks discarding valid and potentially important information. A gap in a histogram is a common and often perfectly explainable feature of real data and does not automatically render an entire dataset unusable or change the underlying scale type of the variable.
  81. The correct answer is A (Mean or median for central tendency, alongside standard deviation or interquartile range for spread.): A thorough initial univariate summary generally pairs a measure of central tendency, such as the mean or median, with a measure of spread, such as the standard deviation or interquartile range, since neither type of statistic alone conveys both aspects of the distribution. The mode alone says nothing about how spread out the data is around that value. Sample size and the minimum and maximum values likewise fail to jointly capture both central tendency and typical spread in a meaningful way.
  82. The correct answer is B (Bin widths should align with the integer values, since fractional bins would misrepresent counts.): Because a discrete count variable can only take whole number values, bin boundaries that split an integer value across two bins would be misleading, so bins are typically set to align exactly with the possible integer outcomes. Treating a discrete count as continuous for plotting purposes can obscure the fact that fractional counts are impossible and misrepresent gaps between valid values. Histograms remain a fully valid and common way to visualize discrete count variables, and a pie chart would be a poor substitute for showing the full shape of the distribution.
  83. The correct answer is A (The positive skewness statistic numerically confirms the right skewed shape seen in the histogram.): A large positive skewness statistic quantitatively supports the same conclusion suggested visually by a histogram with a long right tail, namely that the distribution is right skewed. A negative skewness value would instead suggest left skewness, so a positive value is consistent with, not contradictory to, the visual impression described here. Skewness is a shape descriptor for continuous or discrete numeric variables and has no bearing on whether a variable should be reclassified as ordinal.
  84. The correct answer is D (The histogram reveals overall shape and modality, while the boxplot flags outliers and quartiles.): Histograms are particularly good at revealing the overall shape of a distribution, including skewness and the presence of multiple modes, while boxplots more explicitly summarize quartile positions and flag individual points as potential outliers. These two visualizations complement rather than duplicate one another, since each highlights somewhat different aspects of the same underlying data. Both histograms and boxplots are standard tools specifically for continuous or count variables, not for purely categorical ones, and neither requires the other to be constructed first.
  85. The correct answer is A (Relatively high variability in claim severity relative to its average size, consistent with a heavy tail.): The coefficient of variation standardizes spread relative to the mean, so an unusually high value indicates that claim severities vary substantially relative to their average size, which is often a hallmark of heavy tailed distributions with occasional very large claims. This measure applies directly to ratio scaled continuous variables like claim severity and does not itself indicate anything about ordinal coding. There is no requirement to log transform a variable before its coefficient of variation can be computed, and the statistic itself says nothing directly about the length of the historical time frame used.
  86. The correct answer is B (To understand the shape, spread, and outliers in each variable before deciding how to handle it.): Systematically reviewing histograms and boxplots for each continuous variable early in a project helps an analyst understand distributional shape, spread, and any unusual or extreme values that may need attention before modeling begins. Univariate exploration informs later decisions but does not by itself fully determine the final model form, which typically depends on many additional considerations. This early step also does not eliminate the separate and equally important need to examine bivariate relationships between predictors and the response.
  87. The correct answer is A (Little to no linear association appears to exist between claim severity and policyholder age.): A scatterplot with no discernible upward or downward trend among the points is generally consistent with weak or negligible linear association between the two plotted variables. Scatterplots do reveal patterns when they exist, but a lack of visible pattern here suggests the opposite of a strong relationship, not confirmation of one. There is no requirement that two variables share the same measurement scale before a scatterplot or a correlation assessment can be meaningfully constructed between them.
  88. The correct answer is C (A strong positive linear relationship, though correlation alone does not establish causation.): A Pearson correlation of 0.85 is generally interpreted as indicating a strong positive linear relationship between the two continuous variables. Correlation, however, measures association rather than causation, so this statistic alone cannot establish that changes in one variable directly cause changes in the other. Pearson correlation is specifically designed for continuous variables, and a value of 0.85 is well within the range typically described as strong rather than weak or negligible.
  89. The correct answer is B (A faceted scatterplot, which creates a separate panel for each vehicle type while keeping axes comparable.): Faceting, also called small multiples, creates a separate panel of the same plot type for each level of a grouping variable, allowing a direct visual comparison of the vehicle age and claim severity relationship across vehicle types on comparable axes. A single combined pie chart could not display a bivariate continuous relationship at all. Restricting the analysis to a univariate histogram of vehicle age alone, or to a single overall mean, would discard exactly the kind of subgroup comparison the analyst is trying to make.
  90. The correct answer is C (To examine whether claim occurrence rates differ across coverage tiers by comparing counts.): A cross tabulation, or contingency table, displays the joint frequency of two categorical variables, letting an analyst compare claim occurrence counts or proportions across the different coverage tiers to look for apparent association. Standard Pearson correlation is designed for continuous variables and is not typically computed directly from raw category labels without additional steps such as encoding. Constructing a cross tabulation does not convert the underlying variables to continuous type, nor does it remove the value of also examining each variable individually.
  91. The correct answer is A (It suggests a simple linear correlation measure may misrepresent the true relationship between the variables.): Pearson correlation specifically measures the strength of a linear relationship, so a clearly curved pattern in a scatterplot signals that this single numeric summary may fail to capture the true, non-linear nature of the association between the variables. Observing non-linearity is a reason to consider transformations or non-linear modeling approaches, not necessarily a reason to discard the predictor entirely. Recognizing this limitation of correlation is precisely why visual inspection through scatterplots remains an essential complement to numeric summary statistics.
  92. The correct answer is B (It allows direct visual comparison of medians, spreads, and outliers across regions on one scale.): Placing boxplots for each region side by side on a shared axis makes it straightforward to compare medians, interquartile ranges, and outliers across groups at a glance, which is harder to do when scanning several separate histograms individually. This grouped visualization is a bivariate exploration technique precisely because it examines how a continuous variable relates to a categorical grouping variable, but it does not eliminate the value of also having examined claim severity on its own earlier. Constructing this plot has no bearing on whether region and severity happen to be statistically independent, nor does it change region's fundamentally nominal scale type.
  93. The correct answer is A (Possible multicollinearity, since two highly correlated predictors may provide largely redundant information to a model.): A high correlation between two predictors, such as 0.9 here, suggests they carry substantially overlapping information, which can create multicollinearity issues in certain models and complicate interpretation of individual predictor effects. This finding motivates careful consideration of which variable to retain, combine, or transform, rather than an automatic requirement to discard both entirely. A strong correlation reflects association and does not by itself establish that one variable causes the other, nor does it change either variable's fundamentally continuous nature.
  94. The correct answer is D (It efficiently surfaces multiple pairwise relationships and patterns at once, guiding which variables warrant closer inspection.): A scatterplot matrix arranges every pairwise scatterplot among a set of variables into one compact grid, letting an analyst efficiently scan for interesting patterns, non-linear relationships, or unusual clusters across many variable pairs at once rather than generating and reviewing each plot separately. This exploratory tool does not itself produce a finished predictive model, nor does it remove the value of also computing numeric correlation coefficients to complement the visual impression. The underlying variables remain continuous throughout this process and are not combined into a single categorical variable.
  95. The correct answer is A (Little apparent association between gender and claim type in this dataset, for these categories.): When the proportional breakdown of one categorical variable, here claim type, looks nearly identical across the categories of another variable, here gender, this pattern suggests the two variables show little apparent association in this particular dataset. Nearly identical proportions across groups is generally the opposite of a strong association, not evidence supporting one. Gender remains appropriately treated as a categorical variable in this context, and cross tabulations are in fact a standard and appropriate technique for comparing two categorical variables, including a categorical response like claim type.
  96. The correct answer is C (It can reveal non-linear patterns in the relationship that a straight line would miss.): A loess or other locally weighted smoothing curve can flexibly follow curvature and local trends in the data, revealing non-linear patterns that a single straight regression line, which assumes a constant linear relationship, would necessarily miss or average over. Adding a smoothed curve to a plot has no direct effect on any correlation coefficient computed separately from the raw data. The underlying premium and age variables remain continuous throughout, and examining the raw scattered points alongside the smoothed curve remains valuable rather than unnecessary.
  97. The correct answer is D (A correlation coefficient alone cannot reveal non-linear patterns or the influence of individual unusual points.): A single correlation coefficient summarizes only the strength and direction of a linear relationship and can be heavily influenced by a small number of unusual points, so it cannot reveal curvature, clusters, or the specific influence of individual observations the way a scatterplot can. This limitation holds regardless of the actual numeric value of the correlation coefficient, not only when it happens to equal zero. There is no requirement to compute a correlation coefficient before constructing a scatterplot; the two are complementary, independent tools for bivariate exploration.
  98. The correct answer is B (A gradual shift in the center or spread of the severity distribution across successive policy years.): A gradual, consistent shift in the center, spread, or shape of the severity distribution as policy year increases is exactly the kind of pattern that would suggest a genuine trend, such as inflation, worth investigating further. Identical distributions across all facets would instead suggest the absence of any meaningful trend over time. A single isolated outlier in one year's facet is a much narrower observation than a broader trend and does not by itself establish any systematic pattern across the six years.
  99. The correct answer is D (A faceted scatterplot splitting the data by prior accident status while plotting experience against frequency.): Splitting a scatterplot of experience against claim frequency into separate groups or facets based on prior at fault accident status directly allows the analyst to see whether the relationship between these two variables differs across that additional categorical dimension. A univariate histogram of experience alone would say nothing about its relationship with claim frequency or about the role of prior accidents. A pie chart of accident proportions alone, or a cross tabulation restricted to two nominal variables, would not capture the specific numeric relationship the analyst wants to explore here.
  100. This sensitivity to influential points is a well known and entirely valid property of the Pearson correlation statistic rather than a sign of a computational error. This finding does not change household driver count's fundamentally discrete numeric nature, and it clearly warrants further investigation rather than being dismissed.

Two separate histograms would show each variable's marginal distribution but not their relationship to each other. A pie chart is unsuited to continuous data entirely. A single bar chart of averages loses the individual-level pattern that the scatterplot preserves.
  80. The correct answer is B (Angle judgments in pie charts are harder to compare accurately than bar lengths): human perception is generally more accurate at judging linear length than angular area, which is why bar charts are often preferred over pie charts for part-to-whole comparisons. This is a well established finding in graphical perception research applied to good visualization design. Bar charts handle any number of categories and are not restricted to time series use, contrary to the other distractors. Pie charts do not require continuous data either, so that option misstates the actual limitation.
  81. The correct answer is D (A detailed table of the forty exact values): when the goal is precise lookup of exact numeric values rather than pattern recognition, a table is generally more effective than a chart. Charts excel at revealing overall patterns and comparisons but sacrifice precision for readability. A bar chart with forty bars would be cluttered and still less precise than tabulated numbers. A pie chart with forty slices would be nearly unreadable and is unsuited to this precision requirement.
  82. The correct answer is B (A multi-line chart with one distinctly colored line per product, which would directly reveal how the trends diverge): plotting all three product lines as separate colored lines on a shared time axis lets viewers see each trend and how the lines diverge or converge over the five years. A monthly pie chart repeated many times would be unwieldy and would not show trend well. A single combined histogram loses the time dimension entirely. A boxplot at one point in time cannot show change over five years, so it fails the stated goal of comparing trends.
  83. The correct answer is B (A scatterplot of claim cost against driver age): plotting the response against the predictor directly shows whether the cloud of points follows a roughly straight-line pattern, which is exactly what is needed to assess linearity. A pie chart or bar chart of averages by bracket would obscure the underlying continuous relationship and any nonlinearity within brackets. A stacked bar chart of quartiles is designed for categorical composition, not for assessing a linear trend between two continuous variables.
  84. The correct answer is D (Sorting the bars by loss ratio value instead of alphabetically): ordering bars by their value rather than by an arbitrary label makes rank order immediately visible to the reader, which directly serves the stated goal. Random coloring adds no informative value and can be a form of chartjunk. A 3D perspective effect distorts perceived bar height and should generally be avoided. Switching to a pie chart would make rank ordering harder to perceive, not easier.
  85. The correct answer is A (A line chart plotting claim count against month over the full period): a line chart across the full 36-month period preserves the time ordering needed to see both a repeating seasonal cycle and the overall long-run trend simultaneously. A single aggregated bar collapses away the pattern entirely. A pie chart of claims by calendar month would mix data from different years together and obscure the trend component. A scatterplot against an arbitrary index would lose the meaningful calendar structure that reveals seasonality.
  86. The correct answer is B (They add visual clutter that distracts from the actual data being shown): chartjunk refers to decorative elements that do not encode data and instead compete with or obscure the actual values being communicated. The concern is about clarity and effective communication, not copyright, computing power, or print size, which are unrelated to the core critique. Good graph design favors a high ratio of data-carrying ink to decorative ink.
  87. The correct answer is D (A truncated bar chart where the vertical axis starts above zero, exaggerating the visual difference): truncating the axis breaks the proportional relationship between bar height and underlying value, so the visual difference no longer matches the true magnitude of difference. A standard bar chart with a zero baseline correctly preserves proportional ink. A table does not use ink to represent magnitude visually in the same sense, so it is not the violation being described here.
  88. The correct answer is B (The perspective tilt makes some slices appear larger or smaller than their true share): 3D perspective effects distort the apparent size of pie slices depending on their position and the viewing angle, misrepresenting the underlying proportions. This is a well documented criticism of 3D pie charts in data visualization guidance. The other options describe false claims about accuracy, legality, or category limits that are not the actual concern here.
  89. The correct answer is A (Maximizing the data-to-ink ratio so the chart communicates efficiently): removing gridlines, shadows, and decorative backgrounds that do not encode data increases the proportion of ink devoted to actual information, a core principle of effective, uncluttered graph design. This makes the chart easier to read quickly and reduces distraction from the underlying comparison. Making the file size as large as possible for archival purposes has nothing to do with visual design efficiency. The other remaining options describe goals unrelated to sound visualization practice.
  90. The correct answer is B (Larger counts appear disproportionately larger because area grows with the square of radius): when radius is scaled linearly to a value but the eye perceives area, a bubble twice the true radius appears roughly four times the visual size, distorting perceived magnitude. This is a common and well known bubble chart pitfall in visualization guidance. The correct fix is to scale area, not radius, to the underlying value. The other options misdescribe the mechanism or its consequences.
  91. The correct answer is D (Clip art sized by eye fails to encode the values accurately, misleading the viewer about relative magnitude): when icon size is chosen visually rather than mathematically tied to the data, the resulting comparison misrepresents the true relative values, which undermines the chart's basic communicative purpose. This is a core objection to decorative pictographic charts built without careful scaling. The other options describe unrelated or fabricated restrictions that are not the real issue.
  92. The correct answer is C (Chartjunk that does not contribute to conveying the data): removing unneeded borders, redundant legends, and extra tick marks is a classic example of stripping away chartjunk to leave only elements that serve the reader's understanding of the data. This editing does not change the sample size, the number of variables plotted, or any statistical measure, since it only affects the graphic's visual presentation.
  93. The correct answer is D (Visual elements that do not encode data should not compete with elements that do): a textured background is a non-data-encoding element that interferes with reading the actual data line, violating the principle that decoration should never obscure or compete with the informative content of a chart. The other options make false claims about legality, accuracy, or color requirements that are not the actual design concern.
  94. The correct answer is C (It exaggerates the visual magnitude of relatively small differences between bars): starting the axis well above zero stretches the visible range of a narrow band of values, making modest differences look much larger than they truly are. This is a classic misleading axis technique that violates the proportional ink principle. The other options describe unrelated and false technical limitations that have nothing to do with the real distortion at play.
  95. The correct answer is A (Viewers may misread which axis applies to which line and infer a false relationship between the two series): dual-axis charts are notoriously prone to misinterpretation because the visual overlap of two differently scaled lines can suggest a correlation that does not actually exist, especially without clear labeling. This is a well documented visualization pitfall. The other options describe fabricated technical limitations unrelated to the genuine interpretive risk.
  96. The correct answer is A (Uneven breakpoints can visually exaggerate or minimize real differences between states depending on where the cut points fall): choosing breakpoints that are not evenly or meaningfully spaced can make arbitrary groupings appear as dramatic differences or conceal genuine ones, undermining honest representation of the data. Choropleth map design guidance specifically warns against manipulating class breaks this way. The other options make false or irrelevant claims about map capability.
  97. The correct answer is B (Axes representing a continuous scale like time should maintain consistent, undistorted spacing): compressing part of a time axis unevenly breaks the assumption that equal distances represent equal amounts of time, which distorts the visual rate of change and can mislead viewers about how dramatic a recent trend truly is. The other options describe fabricated rules about logarithmic axes or category restrictions that do not reflect real graph design principles.
  98. The correct answer is D (Adding a violin plot or histogram alongside the boxplot to show underlying distribution shape): boxplots summarize a distribution through quartiles and do not reveal features like bimodality, so supplementing with a violin plot or histogram restores that detail while retaining the boxplot's easy group comparison. Reducing the display to a mean-only table would lose even more information, not less. Removing whiskers or switching to a pie chart would not address the stated concern about hidden distribution shape.
  99. The correct answer is D (Observations flagged as potential outliers beyond a set multiple of the interquartile range): standard boxplot construction plots individual points separately when they fall beyond a common threshold, typically 1.5 times the interquartile range past the nearest quartile, flagging them as potential outliers for further review. These points are not automatically duplicate entries, nor do they represent the median, mean, or lower quartile, which are shown by the box and its center line instead.
  100. The correct answer is A (It aligns medians, quartiles, and outlier points on a common scale so groups can be compared directly): placing boxplots side by side on a shared vertical scale lets a viewer directly compare central tendency, spread, and outlier patterns across the three underwriting years in one glance. Boxplots intentionally summarize rather than show every individual claim value. They also do not eliminate the relevance of sample size or compute a regression line automatically.

Practice Test 5 Answer Key

This pattern does not indicate symmetry, and it does not by itself guarantee any particular ordering of mean versus median without further calculation, so the boxplot alone cannot definitively establish that relationship.

There is no universal fixed number of bins that works for every dataset. Wider bins do not always reveal more true structure, since they can just as easily obscure it.

A pie chart is not designed to reveal distributional shape, and deleting the variable would remove potentially valuable information rather than clarify it.

The correct answer is B (A right-skewed distribution with most claims small and a few very large claims): a tall bar near zero combined with a long, thin tail extending to the right is the textbook description of right skew, which is typical of claim severity data where most claims are modest but a small number are very large. This shape is neither symmetric nor uniform, and it is the opposite of left-skewed, which would instead show a tail extending toward low values with a concentration near the high end.
  8. This technique does not remove the need to choose a bin width, nor does it guarantee the two distributions will look the same, nor does it change the continuous nature of claim frequency into a category.

This is a sample size and bin width interaction, not proof of an unmodelable process or a data error, and histograms can technically be built with any sample size, though small samples require caution in interpretation.

This transformation does not remove outliers outright, nor does it convert continuous data into ordinal categories, and it does not guarantee an exactly normal distribution, only a generally more symmetric one in many practical cases.

Automatically deleting the value, replacing the whole dataset with the median, or assuming fraud are all premature actions that skip the necessary verification step.

This explains why the mean typically exceeds the median in right-skewed data. The other options make false or overly rigid claims about how mean and median must relate.

Automatically deleting or replacing a confirmed legitimate value would discard real information, and ignoring it without any documented consideration would be an incomplete response.

The mean and median are not generally identical except in special symmetric cases, and skewness does not prevent the median from being computed.

This combination does not guarantee normality, nor does it eliminate the value of graphical exploration, nor does it change the variable's underlying measurement scale.

The maximum value or a sum divided by the maximum are not standard measures of central tendency at all.

The other options make false claims that categorical data must be converted first or that the mode always equals the mean, and the claim about a two-category limit for the median is fabricated.

This distinction has nothing to do with requiring identical measurement scales for predictors and responses, and both predictors and responses can indeed be continuous or visualized graphically.

This concern is entirely about data design and quality, not about chart color schemes or chart type choices, and dismissing such issues as never affecting model results would be a serious and incorrect oversimplification.

This decision occurs well before any histogram bin width is chosen, before any specific chart type like a scatterplot or boxplot is selected for reporting, and it does not concern whether the response variable is nominal or ordinal.

Recognizing this shape helps the analyst anticipate that mean based summaries may overstate the typical value.
