Removing exposure from the model entirely would eliminate a variable central to pricing an umbrella policy. Annual data is not restricted to pie chart visualization; it can be shown through many chart types. Monthly interpolation does not guarantee perfect accuracy, since it is fundamentally an estimation method rather than a direct measurement.
  87. The correct answer is A (Map and reconcile the fields from both systems into a single consistent structure): before any meaningful exploration can occur, the analyst must identify which columns in each system represent the same underlying concept and map them into one consistent structure. Assuming the systems already use identical column names contradicts the premise that they use different naming conventions. Discarding the legacy system data assumes it is inferior without justification, when it may hold valuable historical information. Combining the files based on row counts alone ignores the actual need to align column meanings correctly.
  88. The correct answer is D (That the categorization scheme is likely too coarse and may need refinement or recoding to be useful): when nearly half of all values fall into a catch all 'other' category, the underlying categorization scheme is probably too coarse to be analytically useful and likely needs refinement or recoding into more specific categories. It is not accurate to say the variable is perfectly suited for modeling exactly as recorded when it carries so little specific information. Cancellation reason remains fundamentally a categorical concept and does not become continuous simply because one category dominates. A large 'other' category does not necessarily mean the data has been corrupted; it more often reflects an inadequate coding scheme.
  89. The correct answer is D (It captures a meaningful relationship between the two dates that neither date alone conveys, such as claims filed shortly after inception): the elapsed time between policy effective date and claim filing date can reveal suspicious patterns, such as claims filed very shortly after coverage begins, that would not be apparent from either date examined in isolation. Raw dates are routinely stored in structured databases, so that claim is inaccurate. Derived variables are not automatically continuous by definition; they can take many forms depending on how they are constructed. It is not true that effective date and claim date are always identical, since claims typically occur well after a policy's inception.
  90. The correct answer is C (Slightly unequal quarter lengths can distort simple counts unless exposure is measured consistently, such as per day): a quarter containing an extra leap day is very slightly longer than others, and comparing raw claim counts across quarters without adjusting for this can subtly distort the comparison unless exposure is expressed on a consistent basis such as per day. This issue can affect count based measures, not only continuous variables. A single leap day does not come close to doubling the number of claims recorded in a quarter. Quarterly aggregation still requires careful consideration of exposure; it does not eliminate that need.
  91. The correct answer is A (Examining the distribution through a histogram along with mean, median, and spread): a continuous credit based insurance score is well suited to standard univariate numeric summaries, including a histogram to show its shape along with measures like mean, median, and spread. Treating the field only as a nominal category discards the meaningful numeric ordering and scale of the score. Ignoring the field entirely would waste a variable that is fully summarizable using standard numeric methods. Converting the field into unstructured text would strip away the very numeric structure that makes it useful for analysis.
  92. The correct answer is B (Precision of the exposure measure against data availability across the full population): miles driven is a more precise measure of true exposure but is only available where telematics devices are installed, while car years is cruder but universally available, making this a tradeoff between precision and data availability. Removing exposure from the model entirely would eliminate a foundational rating variable rather than resolve the tradeoff. Miles driven can be visualized using many chart types and is not restricted to pie charts. There is no fixed rule that car years is always numerically larger than miles driven, since the two measure fundamentally different units.
  93. The correct answer is C (A U shaped or non-monotonic relationship between age and frequency): higher frequency at both the youngest and oldest ages, with lower frequency in between, describes a U shaped or non-monotonic pattern rather than a simple increasing or decreasing trend. A perfectly linear increasing relationship would show frequency rising steadily across the whole age range, which contradicts the described pattern. The description clearly indicates some relationship exists between age and frequency, so claiming no relationship at all is incorrect. This kind of nonlinear pattern can be captured by a smoothed scatterplot trend line, not only by a bar chart.
  94. The correct answer is B (Excluding them would bias the sample by removing information relevant to understanding renewal behavior): leaving out lapsed policies would bias the training sample toward only those who renewed, removing exactly the information needed to understand what distinguishes policies that lapse from those that do not. It is not accurate that lapsed and renewed policies always share identical characteristics, since differences between them are often what the model is trying to learn. There is no inherent storage limitation preventing lapsed and renewed policies from being kept in the same table. Lapsed policies can certainly contain claim history accumulated before the lapse occurred.
  95. The correct answer is D (Treating this coded field as a continuous numeric variable when it is actually nominal categorical): numeric codes like 1, 2, and 3 assigned to check, direct deposit, and wire transfer represent unordered categories, and the mistake to avoid is treating these codes as if they carried meaningful numeric or continuous properties. It is incorrect to recognize the codes as properly continuous, since arithmetic operations on them would be meaningless. There is no basis for assuming wire transfer is three times more common than check simply because of its numeric code. The field can still be used in models once correctly recoded as a categorical variable, so it is not unusable.
  96. The correct answer is A (Mid term changes in coverage or risk that would otherwise be averaged away in an annual figure): tracking exposure monthly with mid term changes recorded separately captures shifts in coverage or risk that occur partway through the year, detail that a single annual exposure figure would smooth over and lose. It is not accurate that annual and monthly exposure always produce identical model results, since the finer granularity can reveal patterns the coarser measure misses. Claim payment method is an unrelated variable and has no connection to exposure granularity. Communication preference is likewise unrelated to how exposure timing is measured.
  97. The correct answer is A (Whether the differing legal definitions create genuinely comparable outcome measures across states, or require separate treatment): since disability duration thresholds differ by state law, the analyst must confirm whether claim durations across states actually measure the same underlying concept before pooling them, or whether state specific treatment is needed. Dropping state as irrelevant ignores a factor the scenario explicitly identifies as legally significant. Claim durations are not restricted to pie chart visualization; many chart types can display duration data. Assuming all states use identical definitions without checking is precisely the risky shortcut this question warns against.
  98. The correct answer is D (That the data within the interquartile range is skewed toward the higher values, since more of the range sits above the median): when the median sits closer to the bottom of the box, a larger portion of the interquartile range lies above it than below it, indicating that the middle fifty percent of the data is skewed toward higher premium values. This pattern is the opposite of perfect symmetry within that range. It does not imply that every value in the box is identical, since a real spread of values still exists on both sides of the median. A boxplot conveys meaningful information about spread and skew on its own and does not require a corresponding scatterplot to be interpreted.
  99. The correct answer is D (The loss date, since it reflects when the underlying weather or plumbing event actually occurred): seasonal patterns in water damage are driven by when the physical event, such as a freeze or heavy rain, actually happened, which is captured by the loss date rather than whatever later date the claim happened to be reported. Claiming the report date is always recorded more quickly than the loss date is not a reliable general assumption, and even if true, it would not reflect true seasonality of the underlying event. It is not accurate that seasonality cannot be studied using claims data, since that is exactly the kind of pattern such data can reveal when the right date field is used. Assuming report dates are always the only accurately stored dates overstates a limitation that does not generally apply to structured claims systems.
  100. The correct answer is C (The geographic and temporal keys, such as region and date range, must be consistently defined across both tables for a correct join): correctly flagging exposure to a catastrophe event requires that region definitions and date ranges be consistently defined and matched between the policy table and the event lookup table, or policies could be incorrectly flagged or missed entirely. File size has no bearing on whether a join correctly identifies exposed policies. Column order within each table does not need to match for a join to work correctly, since joins are performed on key values rather than column position. Assuming any join will automatically produce correct flags ignores the real risk of mismatched or inconsistently defined keys between the two tables.

Practice Test 7 Answer Key

  1. The correct answer is D (Binning can capture nonlinear age effects but loses within bin granularity): grouping a continuous variable into bins lets a linear model fit a different level for each group, which can flexibly approximate a nonlinear relationship between age and loss cost. The tradeoff is that every observation within a bin, whether near the low or high edge, is treated identically, so information about the precise value is discarded. This can reduce the model's ability to distinguish risks that fall near a bin boundary. The choice between binning and a continuous or spline based term always involves weighing this flexibility against the loss of granularity.
  2. The correct answer is D (Add an interaction term between prior claims and driver age group): when the effect of one predictor on the response genuinely depends on the level of another predictor, a main effects only model cannot represent that dependency. An interaction term multiplies the two variables together, allowing the fitted slope for prior claims to differ across age groups. Standardizing or log transforming prior claims alone would not address the fact that its relationship with the response changes by age. Dropping the variable would remove information the actuary explicitly wants to use in pricing.
  3. The correct answer is C (It expresses relative claim experience on a common comparable scale): a loss ratio divides incurred losses by earned premium, converting two raw dollar amounts into a single relative measure that can be compared fairly across policies of very different sizes. This makes it far more useful for identifying policies with poor experience than looking at total losses alone, which is confounded by policy size. The transformation does not remove outlier claims or guarantee normality, since large losses can still push the ratio to an extreme value. It also does not eliminate the value of examining premium separately for other purposes.
  4. The correct answer is D (It reduces the impact of extreme values and stabilizes variance): a log transform compresses the scale of large values relative to small ones, which dampens the influence of extreme claim amounts and stabilizes variance across the range of the variable. It does not remove any claims from the data, contrary to option C. It does not convert a numeric variable into a categorical one, and it does not change the underlying units of measurement into an unrelated scale with no statistical purpose.
  5. The correct answer is D (One hot encoding, since it avoids implying a false rank order): vehicle body type has no inherent ordering among sedan, SUV, and pickup, so assigning arbitrary integers through ordinal encoding would incorrectly suggest that one category is numerically greater than another. One hot encoding instead creates a separate indicator variable for each level, treating them as independent without implying any order. Using raw frequency counts would introduce an unrelated numeric scale tied to sample size rather than the categorical meaning itself. Leaving the variable as unencoded text is generally not usable directly inside a standard linear model's design matrix.
  6. The correct answer is B (It can leak response information and overfit sparsely populated levels): target encoding replaces each category with a statistic computed from the training response, so any level with very few observations can end up encoded almost entirely by the noise in those few response values rather than a stable underlying signal. This creates a real risk that the model learns patterns specific to the training sample rather than a generalizable relationship. The number of levels the technique can handle is not itself limited to ten, and it does not by itself increase the count of model parameters, since it collapses each level into a single numeric value. Careful validation, such as cross fitting the encoding, is typically needed to control this risk.
  7. The correct answer is A (Perfect multicollinearity, since the dummies sum to the intercept column): when every level of a categorical variable is given its own dummy indicator alongside an intercept, the dummy columns sum to a constant equal to the intercept column, creating perfect linear dependence among the predictors, the classic dummy variable trap. It does not cause a general convergence failure unrelated to this specific singularity. It does not leave the response undefined for any level, and it does not force residuals toward a nonzero mean by itself.
  8. The correct answer is A (Ordinal encoding, since the categories follow a meaningful natural order): education level has a clear inherent progression from less than high school through bachelor's degree or higher, so representing that order with increasing integer codes preserves real information the model can use, such as a monotonic relationship with the response. One hot encoding would discard this ordering information by treating every level as unrelated to the others. Assigning random unrelated numbers would break the meaningful sequence entirely. Dropping the variable would discard a predictor that carries genuine and encodable structure.
  9. The correct answer is A (Add a small positive constant to the variable before taking the log): since the logarithm of zero is undefined, a common and simple fix is to shift the variable by adding a small positive constant, commonly one, before applying the transformation, which keeps zero claim policies in the dataset while making the log operation well defined. Deleting those policies would discard real observations and could bias the analysis. Replacing zeros with the sample mean would distort the true count for those policies rather than solve the mathematical issue. Converting the variable to categorical abandons the log transform approach entirely rather than fixing it.
  10. The correct answer is D (It captures how the credit score effect changes across territories): including territory as a main effect alongside an interaction between territory and credit score allows the slope associated with credit score to differ depending on which territory a policy is in. This lets the model represent situations where credit score matters more strongly in some territories than others. The interaction coefficient itself is not simply the overall average territory effect, and it does not measure the raw correlation between the two variables. It also does not eliminate the ongoing need for a separate main effect term for credit score in the model.
  11. The correct answer is A (Two policies near opposite ends of one bin are treated identically): once mileage is grouped into ranges such as under ten thousand or ten to twenty thousand miles, any two policies that both fall within the same bin receive the exact same fitted effect, even if one is near the very bottom of the range and the other near the very top. This loss of within bin distinction is the core cost of binning relative to a continuous specification. Binned variables can absolutely be included in a GLM design matrix through dummy coding, so that claim is false. Binning does not universally produce a worse fit or automatically strip away statistical significance.
  12. The correct answer is B (It puts claim experience on a comparable per unit exposure basis): dividing claim counts by earned exposure adjusts for the fact that policies can be observed for different lengths of time, so a policy earned for a full year and one earned for only a few months become directly comparable once expressed per unit of exposure. This is not a binary indicator, since it produces a continuous rate rather than a yes or no flag. Creating this ratio does not remove the general need to consider standardizing other unrelated predictors, and the resulting frequency variable is not guaranteed to follow a normal distribution, since it often remains right skewed.
  13. The correct answer is A (Distance based or regularized methods can be dominated by scale differences): a ratio such as average severity per policy can end up on a very different numeric scale than raw counts or dollar amounts left untransformed, and methods that rely on distances or that penalize coefficient magnitudes, such as k means or ridge regression, can be disproportionately influenced by whichever variable happens to have the largest scale. This does not remove the ability to interpret the ratio in dollar terms, since the units are still well defined. GLMs are able to accept features created through division without restriction, and the ratio is not automatically perfectly collinear with total losses, since it also depends on claim count.
  14. The correct answer is D (To reduce noisy, unstable coefficient estimates from sparse levels): when many categorical levels each contain only a handful of observations, estimating a separate effect for every one of them produces highly unstable coefficients driven largely by sampling noise rather than genuine signal. Grouping the rarest levels into a single other category pools enough observations together to produce a more stable and generalizable estimate. This grouping reduces the number of distinct categories rather than increasing it, and it does not convert a nominal variable into an ordinal one. It also does not prevent the resulting grouped variable from being used in later interaction terms.
  15. The correct answer is D (It reduces heteroskedasticity and the leverage of extreme large claims): compressing large values more than small ones through a log transform tends to make the spread of residuals more uniform across the range of fitted values and limits how much influence a small number of very large claims can exert on the fitted model. It does not turn severity into a categorical predictor, since the transformed variable remains continuous. A lower mean squared error is not guaranteed on every future dataset, since transformation benefits depend on the true underlying relationship. This transformation also does not remove the ongoing need to validate the model on holdout data.
  16. The correct answer is A (A different slope for the experience variable within each policy type): interacting a categorical variable with a continuous one allows the continuous variable's estimated slope to vary depending on which category of the categorical variable applies, so personal and commercial policies can each have their own experience effect. This is different from forcing one shared slope for experience across the entire dataset. Including this interaction does not remove years of experience from the fitted model, since a main effect for it typically remains alongside the interaction. It also does not by itself guarantee that personal and commercial policies share equal loss cost overall.
  17. The correct answer is B (It risks overfitting through features found by chance rather than substance): exhaustively generating many combinations and keeping whichever ones correlate most strongly with the training response tends to capture patterns that exist only by random chance in that specific sample, rather than reflecting a real and generalizable relationship. This does not guarantee that every selected feature will be actuarially interpretable, since purely statistical selection can surface combinations with no sensible business meaning. It also does not remove multicollinearity from the resulting set, since correlated combinations can easily survive this kind of selection. Out of sample validation remains essential precisely because of this overfitting risk, not something the approach eliminates.
  18. The correct answer is B (Equal width bins split the range evenly, while equal frequency balances counts): equal width binning divides the full range of the variable into intervals of the same numeric width regardless of how many observations fall in each, while equal frequency binning instead chooses interval boundaries so that roughly the same number of observations fall into each bin, which can produce bins of very different widths. Neither approach guarantees a linear relationship with the response, since binning is a data grouping choice rather than a statistical guarantee. Equal width binning is not restricted to normally distributed variables, and equal frequency binning is fully applicable to continuous variables rather than only categorical ones.
  19. The correct answer is D (A ratio based derived feature combining two raw predictors): body mass index is constructed by dividing one raw variable, weight, by a function of another raw variable, height squared, which is a direct example of building a new ratio style feature from existing measured predictors. This is not one hot encoding, since no nominal categorical variable is being represented here. It is also not principal components analysis, which would instead construct linear combinations designed to capture maximum variance across many correlated variables rather than a single domain motivated ratio. It likewise has nothing to do with grouping observations through hierarchical clustering.
  20. The correct answer is D (It is the direction in the data that captures the maximum variance): principal components analysis constructs each successive component as the linear combination of the original variables that explains as much of the remaining variance as possible, subject to being uncorrelated with earlier components, and the first component in particular captures more variance than any other single linear combination. It is not defined as the single original variable with the least correlation to the others, since it is a combination of many variables rather than one variable chosen from the set. It is not a randomly chosen combination, since it is derived through an optimization based on the variance structure of the data. It is also not simply the average of all original variables, since the weights on each variable are determined by the data rather than fixed to be equal.
  21. The correct answer is D (Without standardizing, the variable with the largest scale can dominate the components): PCA operates on the variance of each variable, so a predictor measured in thousands of dollars will naturally have far larger variance in raw units than a variable measured in single years, and without rescaling, the components will end up dominated by whichever variable happens to have the largest numeric scale rather than whichever is most informative. Standardizing before PCA does not itself cause a large variance variable to dominate, since that is precisely the problem standardization is meant to prevent. Standardization is not required only for categorical variables, since PCA is generally applied to continuous data in the first place. It also does not guarantee that the first component alone will explain all of the total variance.
  22. The correct answer is C (They show how strongly each original variable contributes to that component): loadings represent the weights applied to each original variable when constructing a given principal component, so large positive loadings on debt ratio, leverage ratio, and interest coverage inverse indicate these variables move together strongly and contribute heavily to that component. Loadings do not represent correlation with a separate response variable, since PCA is computed without reference to any response. They also do not indicate the number of clusters that should be formed in a later clustering step. Finding large loadings on a set of variables does not by itself confirm those variables must be dropped from any future model.
  23. The correct answer is D (To decide how many principal components capture most of the meaningful variance): a scree plot displays the variance explained by each successive component in decreasing order, and the elbow marks the point where additional components begin to add only marginal explanatory value, providing a practical rule of thumb for how many components to retain. This process is unrelated to determining how many original variables were categorical, since PCA is typically applied to continuous variables from the outset. It also does not calculate the exact number of clusters needed for a later k means analysis, which is a separate decision made using its own methods. Identifying the elbow likewise does not confirm anything about whether variables were measured on the same scale.
  24. The correct answer is A (The cumulative proportion of variance explained by those three components): reporting that the first three components together explain seventy eight percent of total variance describes the cumulative proportion of variance explained, summing the individual contribution of each of those components. This figure is unrelated to how many policies would later be correctly classified by a cluster analysis, since PCA and clustering serve different purposes. It is also not a correlation coefficient between the first and second components, since those components are uncorrelated by construction. This percentage does not represent an improvement in predictive accuracy over a linear model either, since PCA alone does not fit any predictive model.
  25. The correct answer is A (PCA is unsupervised and constructs components without using the response variable): PCA works purely with the covariance or correlation structure among the predictor variables themselves and does not reference any labeled outcome when determining the components, which is why it is classified as an unsupervised technique. It does not require a labeled response variable to compute its components, contrary to the second option. PCA also does not select a subset of predictors based on correlation with a response, since that would describe a supervised feature selection method rather than PCA. It likewise does not replace the response variable with any weighted average of predictors.
  26. The correct answer is C (It fixes the scale of the loading vectors so components are comparable): requiring the squared loadings within each component's vector to sum to one is a normalization convention that fixes the length of that vector, ensuring loadings can be meaningfully compared across different components and across different variables within the same component. This normalization does not force every individual loading to be positive, since loadings can carry either sign. It also does not require that all original variables have identical variance beforehand, since that is a separate consideration addressed through standardization. Normalizing the loading vector does not convert the loadings into correlation coefficients with any response variable either.
  27. The correct answer is D (Each component is a linear combination of the original predictor variables): every principal component is constructed as a weighted sum of the original variables, with the weights chosen by the PCA procedure to satisfy the variance maximizing and orthogonality properties that define the components. A component is not simply one original variable renamed without recalculation, since it typically draws on information from many variables at once. It is also not a randomly generated variable independent of the data, since the construction is fully determined by the covariance structure of the actual dataset. A principal component is furthermore distinct from a categorical grouping label produced by a separate cluster analysis.
  28. The correct answer is B (PCA components are uncorrelated, which can stabilize the regression fit): when predictors are highly correlated, regression coefficient estimates can become unstable and difficult to interpret, and regressing on the leading principal components instead is helpful because those components are constructed to be uncorrelated with one another, which removes the multicollinearity that was causing the instability. This approach does not guarantee that resulting coefficients become causally interpretable, since PCA regression still reflects associations rather than proven causal effects. It also does not remove the need to check residuals afterward, since diagnostic checking remains an important step. This technique likewise does not convert a continuous response into a categorical outcome.
  29. The correct answer is D (The eigenvalue equals the amount of variance explained by that component): in PCA, each principal component corresponds to an eigenvector of the covariance or correlation matrix, and its associated eigenvalue directly equals the amount of total variance in the data that component accounts for, which is why eigenvalues are used to compute proportion of variance explained. An eigenvalue is not simply a count of how many original variables were used to build the component, since every component can draw on all original variables through its loadings. It is not a p value testing statistical significance, since PCA is a descriptive and dimension reducing technique rather than a hypothesis testing procedure. An eigenvalue also does not directly specify how many clusters the data should ultimately form.
  30. The correct answer is B (The larger scale variable will dominate the components regardless of its true importance): because PCA maximizes variance and raw variance depends heavily on the units and scale of measurement, a variable like total assets measured in millions will contribute far more raw variance than customer age measured in single years, causing the components to be driven primarily by the larger scale variable even if it is not more informative. The resulting components will not be identical to a properly standardized version of the analysis. PCA does not automatically rescale variables internally unless the analyst explicitly requests standardized inputs. The components will also not reflect variation in age alone, since some influence from the dominating variable will still appear.
  31. The correct answer is A (The maximum equals the minimum of the number of observations minus one and the number of variables): the number of meaningful principal components that can be extracted is bounded by the smaller of the number of variables and one less than the number of observations, since the covariance structure cannot support more independent directions of variation than that. It is not simply capped at half the number of predictor variables, since that is not the actual mathematical constraint involved. The maximum is also not fixed at exactly ten components regardless of the dataset's actual size and dimensionality. It is likewise not determined solely by how many categorical variables happen to be present, since PCA is generally applied to continuous inputs.
  32. The correct answer is C (How observations relate to each other and how variables relate to the components): a biplot overlays the scores of individual observations along the first two principal components with arrows showing how strongly and in what direction each original variable loads onto those same two components, allowing both observation level patterns and variable level relationships to be examined together on a single plot. This plot does not show the exact statistical significance of regression coefficients, since it is a descriptive visualization rather than a hypothesis test output. It also does not reveal the precise number of clusters that a separate k means analysis would eventually find. A biplot likewise does not directly indicate whether the response variable follows a normal or skewed distribution.
  33. The correct answer is A (The mathematically optimal components are not always easy to interpret in practice): PCA components are chosen purely to maximize captured variance subject to mathematical constraints, and this optimization can sometimes produce loadings spread across many seemingly unrelated variables with mixed signs, making the resulting component difficult to summarize in plain business language even though it is statistically valid. PCA does not guarantee a clear business interpretation for every component it produces. Mixed sign loadings are a normal and expected outcome of the underlying linear algebra rather than evidence of any computational failure. Encountering mixed signs on unrelated seeming variables also does not by itself indicate a coding error in the dataset.
  34. The correct answer is C (PCA constructs components as linear combinations and can miss nonlinear structure): since every principal component is restricted to being a linear combination of the original variables, PCA is fundamentally limited in its ability to capture curved or otherwise nonlinear relationships among variables, and such structure can be spread across many components or lost altogether rather than concentrated into one interpretable direction. PCA can absolutely be applied to datasets containing more than two variables, so that restriction does not apply. It does not automatically detect and model nonlinear relationships without some other adjustment, such as adding transformed variables beforehand. PCA also does not require the response variable to be included, since it remains an unsupervised technique.
  35. The correct answer is B (A correlation of zero, since principal component scores are uncorrelated): by construction, each successive principal component is required to be orthogonal to, and therefore uncorrelated with, all previously extracted components, so the correlation between the first and second component scores should be zero across the observations. This rules out a strong positive correlation close to one between the two components. The correlation is also not equal to the proportion of variance explained, since those are entirely different quantities computed from different aspects of the decomposition. The correlation between component scores is likewise unrelated to the correlation between whichever two original variables happen to load most heavily.
  36. The correct answer is D (They are two different heuristics that can sometimes suggest a different count): choosing components based on a fixed cumulative variance threshold such as eighty percent and choosing based on the visual elbow in a scree plot are both commonly used rules of thumb, but they rely on different criteria and can reasonably lead to different recommended numbers of components for the same dataset. These two approaches are not mathematically identical procedures guaranteed to always agree, since one is a fixed numeric cutoff and the other is a visual judgment about the shape of the variance curve. Neither approach is invalid outright, since both are widely used heuristics in practice rather than rigorously proven rules. Dismissing either method entirely overstates how strictly justified either threshold or elbow choice actually is.
  37. The correct answer is B (By plotting the scores of the first two principal components against each other): since the first two principal components are constructed to capture as much of the overall variance as possible in just two dimensions, plotting each observation's score on these two components against each other provides a practical two dimensional summary of the broader fifty variable structure that can be visually inspected for patterns or groupings. This visualization does not involve converting categorical variables into a single continuous response, since PCA operates on the predictor variables themselves. It also does not replace the fifty variables with independently drawn random numbers, since the components are derived directly from the actual data. This plotting approach does not assign observations to exactly two predefined clusters either, since PCA itself does not perform clustering.
  38. The correct answer is D (The sign of a principal component's loadings is arbitrary and can flip): because a principal component and its negative both maximize variance equally well in the underlying mathematics, different software implementations can report loadings with opposite signs for the same component while the direction of the underlying axis and the magnitude of every loading remain identical. This outcome does not necessarily indicate a calculation error in either software package, since sign flipping is an expected and harmless feature of PCA computation. It also does not imply that the two datasets analyzed were actually different from one another. This sign difference can occur regardless of whether the data was properly standardized beforehand.
  39. The correct answer is A (The elbow method for selecting an appropriate number of clusters): plotting total within cluster sum of squares against increasing values of k and looking for the point where additional clusters yield only diminishing improvement is the defining feature of the elbow method, a common heuristic for choosing k in k means clustering. This procedure is unrelated to Ward's linkage, which instead governs how clusters merge in hierarchical clustering rather than how many clusters to select in k means. It is also distinct from standardizing variables, which is a separate preprocessing step performed before distances are ever computed. One hot encoding a categorical variable is likewise a different preprocessing task rather than a method for choosing k.
  40. The correct answer is C (The number of clusters k must be specified by the analyst in advance): standard k means clustering requires the analyst to choose the number of clusters before running the algorithm, and techniques like the elbow method or silhouette analysis are used precisely because the algorithm itself does not determine this value automatically. It is therefore incorrect that k means detects the best k without any input, since a specific value must be supplied as a starting condition. K means also does not automatically set k equal to the number of original variables in the dataset. It likewise does not only function correctly when k is fixed at two, since it can be applied with any reasonable number of clusters.
  41. The correct answer is B (It alternates assignment and centroid update steps until the solution stabilizes): the k means algorithm repeatedly assigns each observation to its nearest current centroid and then recalculates each centroid as the average of the points now assigned to it, continuing this two step cycle until cluster assignments no longer change between iterations. This process does not run for only a single fixed pass, since multiple iterations are generally required to reach a stable solution. It also does not require a labeled response variable, since k means clustering is unsupervised and relies only on the predictor variables. The algorithm additionally does not skip the reassignment step, since both assignment and centroid update happen at every iteration.
  42. The correct answer is A (Run the algorithm multiple times with different random starts and keep the best result): because k means can converge to different local solutions depending on where centroids are initially placed, standard practice is to rerun the algorithm several times from different random starting points and select whichever run achieves the lowest total within cluster sum of squares. It is not true that the first run can always be trusted, since initialization genuinely does affect which local solution the algorithm settles into. Switching to hierarchical clustering is not required to address this specific concern, since k means can simply be rerun as many times as needed. Increasing k to a very large number does not resolve the initialization sensitivity issue and instead introduces a separate problem of overly granular clusters.
  43.
